sources.citation: Gatschet, Albert S. (1890). The Klamath Indians of Southwestern Oregon. Washington, D. C.: Government Printing Office. 495+305+519 pp.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: The accented syllable of a word is uttered with a stronger effort of the voice, and frequently with a higher pitch than the syllables surrounding it. Long words have a principal accent and a secondary accent. [...] In Klamath the emphasizing of the radix is the natural and fundamental law of accentuation, but it is so often interfered with by other agencies that it seems rather to be the exception. Many short particles have no accent of their own, and in terms formed by iterative reduplication each of the doubled radicals has an equal right to the accent; so the accentuation is here decided by rhetoric convenience. [...] Long vowels are not always accented; that is, quantity exercises no decisive influence on accentuation.
sources.locator: Grammar, Phonology, 'Accentuation; I; Location of the accent', printed pp. 236-238; quantity section pp. 243-244; secondary accent p. 238; enclisis pp. 240-243
sources.note: Gatschet's system: four competing principles, (1) root accent, (2) secondary accent, (3) quantity, (4) syntactic emphasis. Root accent is the 'fundamental law' but accent 'constantly shifting' (tula/tula, tawipka/tawipka, shnuka/shnuka, prefixes may take accent). Secondary stress stated: 'In words of four syllables or more.. seeks relief by accentuating another of their number by what is called the secondary accent' (p. 238); the secondary accent can level the main accent 'unless its quantity offers resistance' (shliutuapkuga, radix i short). Weight: explicitly denied as decisive, 'Long vowe

sources.citation: DeLancey, Scott (2005). Argument Structure of Klamath Bipartite Stem. Berkeley Linguistic Society 26S. pp. 15-26.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: The paper is on the argument structure of bipartite verb stems (lexical prefixes + change-of-state stems / locative-directive suffixes) and case marking. A search of the full scanned text (11 pages, printed pp. 15-25) finds no occurrence of stress, accent, tone, pitch, prosody, syllable, foot, mora, quantity or phonology; the only hit for 'tone' is the gloss 'stone'. Cited forms mark vowel length with ':' (e.g. blo?a:k, sdoli:, ksodi:l-) but no stress or accent marks appear and nothing is said about them. Nothing bears on the catalog's weight-sensitive stress entry.
